title: szeretném vs. szeretnék: Two Kinds of "I Would Like"

sections.title: The same -né- infix, two different endings
sections.content: You already know szeretnék ("I would like [something]") and tudnál ("you could") from A2 — both are conditional forms built with -na-/-ne- before the personal ending. Like every Hungarian verb, szeret has two conditional versions: an INDEFINITE one for a general, unspecified thing (szeretnék, matching szeretek), and a DEFINITE one for one particular thing you already have in mind (szeretném, matching szeretem). This unit leans heavily on the definite szeretném, so it's worth locking in the contrast before going further.

sections.title: Indefinite vs. definite conditional of szeret
rows: I like (something, general) → I would like (something)
I like it (a specific thing) → I would like it / I wish for it
you like it (specific) → you would like it

items.english: I would like a better job. (general, indefinite)
I would really like it if it worked out. (the whole idea counts as "definite")

sections.content: A hogy-clause or a ha-clause always counts as that one definite "thing" you're wishing for — so whenever szeretném is followed by hogy or ha, it takes the -m ending, never the -k of szeretnék. Szeretnék, hogy... sounds foreign to a Hungarian ear; szeretném, hogy... / szeretném, ha... is what you'll actually hear.
